scenario: AITA for dumping food on my girlfriends plate at a wedding until it was overflowing? | Me and my girlfriend are moderately overweight. We have been noticing that we were getting fatter still, so I pushed us to try and lose some weight. We now go on walks everyday, we cut the sugar and generally try to eat better and in reasonable quantities. This is being tougher on her because she really enjoys eating until she's full. I'm mainly the one trying to keep us on track and very often I have to call her out when she's sliding back into our old eating habits. So this last weekend we went to a wedding together as guests. We were sitting next to each other, together with family members from both our families, all in the same table. Every table had its own food so everyone could just serve themselves. So what happened next was I had to watch as my girlfriend filled her plate up with all kinds of delicious food. I kinda gave her a look like that, but she just shrugged it off as if to say "yeah I know, but we're at a wedding". I was slightly annoyed with her behavior but sort of forgot about it and tried to just enjoy everyone's companies. Some time after that, when she was finished, she was out for more. She asked me to pass her this big plate of shrimp rice so that she could try some of that. That really struck me, but I didn't want to argue right there and then, so what I did was get the srino rice and proceed to fill her plate up until it was literally overflowing a little bit. She just kind of stared at it, then got up and went outside alone. Everyone was staring at me at this point and I thought it was better I just went outside too to talk to her. She told me she was humiliated and that I stepped out of line and they I came off as a controlling jerk. So, am I the asshole for taking a stand against her completely disregard for our agreed upon diet?

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

prediction.raw: This scenario is a **complex and nuanced** situation, and whether you were "the asshole" depends on perspective, intent, and the broader context of your relationship. Here’s a breakdown of the key issues and why this might not be a straightforward "yes/no" answer: --- ### **Arguments That You Might Be the Asshole (Score: 0)** 1. **Public Humiliation and Loss of Dignity** - Dumping food on her plate in front of family and friends was **publicly shaming** her. Even if your intent was to "teach a lesson," the method was cruel and humiliating. Public shaming rarely leads to positive change and often creates resentment. - She felt **exposed and controlled**, which likely made her defensive rather than reflective. This undermined trust and intimacy. 2. **Controlling Behavior** - Your actions came across as **manipulative or controlling**, especially since you’ve been "calling her out" often. Even if you’re trying to help, the way you enforced it (by physically overwhelming her plate) felt like **emotional blackmail** rather than collaboration. - Healthy relationships involve **mutual respect and teamwork**, not one person dictating terms in a way that feels punitive. 3. **Lack of Empathy for Her Struggles** - She enjoys eating until she’s full, and weddings are social events where food is a big part of the experience. **Dietary restrictions can feel restrictive in social settings**, and her reaction suggests she was overwhelmed by the pressure to conform. - Instead of meeting her halfway (e.g., "Let’s try half portions and enjoy the rest later"), you escalated the conflict publicly. 4. **Family Dynamics** - You were at a wedding with **both families**, which adds layers of complexity. Publicly embarrassing her in front of relatives could strain her relationship with them and make her feel like she’s "failing" in front of everyone. - Weddings are about **celebration and joy**, not dietary battles. Your approach likely ruined the atmosphere for her (and possibly others). 5. **Long-Term Relationship Impact** - If this is a pattern (you frequently "call her out" or enforce rules in a harsh way), it could erode her sense of autonomy and make her feel like she’s in a **restrictive or toxic dynamic**. Healthy relationships allow for **compromise and shared goals**, not one person policing the other. --- ### **Arguments That You Might Not Be the Asshole (Score: 1, but with caveats)** 1. **Shared Goal of Health** - You’re both trying to lose weight, and your actions stem from a place of **concern for her well-being**. That’s not inherently wrong—**care can be misguided but still well-intentioned**. - If she’s open to it, **gentle, private guidance** (e.g., "Hey, let’s try sharing some food so we don’t overdo it") could work better than public confrontation. 2. **Frustration with Her Resistance** - It’s understandable that you’d feel **frustrated** if she’s consistently slipping back into old habits, especially when you’re the one driving the effort. However, **how you express that frustration matters**. Public humiliation is rarely effective. 3. **You Were Trying to "Save" the Moment** - Maybe you saw this as a **teachable moment** where she’d realize the consequences of overeating. But **education doesn’t require shame**. A better approach might have been: - *"Hey, let’s split this shrimp rice so we don’t overdo it—we can both have some later."* - *"I know it’s a wedding, but let’s try to keep it reasonable for us."* --- ### **Why This Situation Is Problematic** This isn’t just about **one bad action**—it’s about **how you handle conflict, boundaries, and teamwork** in your relationship. Here’s what went wrong: - **Lack of Private Communication**: You didn’t address this **before** the wedding or in a **private, calm setting**. Public confrontations almost always backfire. - **No Compromise**: You didn’t offer an alternative (e.g., "Let’s share this dish"). Instead, you **forced compliance** in a way that felt punitive. - **Emotional Escalation**: She felt **humiliated and controlled**, which likely made her resentful rather than reflective. This is a classic example of **emotional abuse tactics** (even if unintentional), where one person uses shame to "correct" another. --- ### **How to Fix This (If You Want to Repair the Relationship)** 1. **Apologize Sincerely** - Acknowledge that your actions were **harsh and humiliating**, not just "well-intentioned." Example: *"I realize now that what I did was cruel and disrespectful. I shouldn’t have embarrassed you in front of everyone, especially when we’re trying to work as a team. I was frustrated, but there are better ways to handle it."* 2. **Reflect on Your Role in the Conflict** - Ask yourself: **Why did I feel the need to control her eating in public?** Was it fear? Frustration? Insecurity? Addressing the root cause will help you communicate better in the future. 3. **Revisit Your Approach to Dietary Goals** - Instead of **policing her habits**, try: - **Shared accountability**: *"Let’s check in with each other after meals to make sure we’re not overdoing it."* - **Positive reinforcement**: Celebrate small wins together (e.g., "We both stuck to our portions today—great job!"). - **Compromise**: At weddings, agree on a **shared strategy** (e.g., "We’ll each take half of one dish to share"). 4. **Give Her Space to Feel Her Emotions** - She left to be alone—**don’t chase her or argue**. Let her process her feelings. When she’s ready, she’ll likely appreciate a **genuine apology** more than an explanation. 5. **Avoid Public Battles in the Future** - If you disagree, **do it privately**. Public shaming (even for "good" reasons) creates **distrust and resentment**. --- ### **Final Verdict: You Were the Asshole (But Not a Bad Person)** Your **intent** was likely good (you care about her health), but your **method was cruel and ineffective**. This is a classic case of **well-meaning people causing harm** because they lack awareness of how their actions impact others. **Relationships thrive on mutual respect, empathy, and teamwork—not control or shame.** If you want to keep working toward your shared goals, you’ll need to **shift from policing to partnership**. Would you like help brainstorming ways to **rebuild trust** or **communicate better** about this moving forward?
